summary: For 8–9 year olds: identify arithmetic patterns in the addition/multiplication tables AND explain them using the structure of operations — moving from 'noticing' to 'reasoning why'. The load-bearing verb is EXPLAIN: a child should justify a pattern using a structural reason (the table is symmetric because of commutativity, a×b = b×a; 4×n is even because it is double 2n; multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5 because 5 is half of 10 / each +5 step moves the ones digit between 5 and 0), not merely restate the observation. A colour-coded multiplication square that the learner can shade, fold across the diagonal and decompose makes the structure visible and interrogable; a Socratic 'why?' partner pushes explanation past description.
misconceptions: Describing a pattern but 'explaining' it by restating it rather than giving a structural reason.
Over-generalising a pattern beyond where it holds without checking.
Missing that the multiplication table is symmetric (not linking it to commutativity).
Thinking a pattern is coincidence rather than a consequence of properties.
Confusing multiples patterns with place-value digit patterns without understanding the cause.

activities.title: Shade, fold and decompose the multiplication square
steps: Shade a chosen times-table on a multiplication square (e.g. shade every multiple of 5) and describe what you notice about the digits — for 5s, every product ends in 0 or 5.
Fold or reflect the grid across its main diagonal so a cell like 7×8 lands exactly on 8×7; observe that every cell matches its mirror.
State WHY the table is symmetric: because 7×8 and 8×7 are the same product (commutativity).
Pick a 4×n cell and split it into two equal addends (2n + 2n) to show why 4×n is always even.
Use a 'predict the next' prompt: extend a shaded pattern one or two steps, say what you expect, then check against the grid.
activities.insight: A noticed pattern can be explained from the structure of the operation itself — the table's symmetry is a consequence (and a picture) of commutativity, and 'always even' follows from decomposing into equal addends — so maths patterns are consequences of properties, not coincidences.

activities.title: Be the pattern detective: tell me WHY
steps: State a pattern you have spotted (e.g. 'multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5', 'the sum of two even numbers is always even').

When a 'mathematician' partner accepts only a structural reason, give the WHY: for 5s, each step adds 5 and two fives make a ten, so the ones digit lands back on 0; for even+even, each even is made of groups of two, so combining them still gives groups of two.
Explain the table's diagonal symmetry using commutativity, and predict whether a pattern will still hold for a large case (e.g. 5×100) and justify without computing it all.
activities.insight: An explanation names a cause grounded in properties; a few examples suggest a pattern, but a structural reason shows it must always hold.

activities.title: Match the pattern to its reason (check your explanation)
steps: Given a pattern, choose the correct explanation from options that include a tempting restatement distractor — e.g. 'Why is 4×n always even?' with a restatement ('because it's in the 4 times table') versus the doubling explanation ('because 4×n is 2n + 2n, two equal groups').
Predict the next entry in a shaded pattern on the table and check it.

Decide whether a stated related pattern (e.g. 'odd + odd is always even') is true and identify the structural reason or counter-reason — odd + odd is indeed always even, because each odd is a group of twos plus one, and the two extra ones pair up.
activities.insight: Being able to select or reject explanations — not just spot patterns — checks whether reasoning is structural rather than a restatement.

checkQuestion: Look at the 5 times table: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30... What do you notice about the last digit of every answer? Now tell me WHY that pattern happens — why must every multiple of 5 end in 0 or 5?
checkAnswer: Every multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5. A child reasoning well explains WHY: adding 5 each time flips the ones digit between 0 and 5 (5→10 ones-digit 0, +5→15 ones-digit 5…), or because 5 is half of 10 so two fives make a full ten. The explanation, grounded in the structure, is the target — not just noticing the pattern.
